subject: 만다라의 기하 구조
title: A diagram built outward from a centre
content: A mandala is organised around a central point with concentric enclosures around it, and the arrangement is prescribed rather than composed. Every element occupies the position its meaning assigns, so what looks like a decorative pattern is closer to a plan of a building seen from above. The centre holds the principal figure. Everything else is placed in relation to it, with rank decreasing outward, so a viewer reading the image from the middle outward is following an order that the tradition specifies exactly. Painters work from the centre for this reason. Square within circle is the recurring structure. An inner square with gates on four sides sits inside one or more circles, which is the plan of an enclosure with entrances, and the gates face the cardinal directions so that the whole diagram is oriented. Several such images are explicitly described as buildings in the texts that govern them. Proportion is measured rather than judged. Manuals specify the relationships between elements in units, and a painter lays out a grid before any image appears, so two works made from the same specification centuries apart agree in structure while differing in handling. The grid is drawn and then covered. Colour follows the directional scheme. Each quarter carries the colour its direction requires, so the arrangement of hues is determined before any aesthetic choice is made, and a painter's judgement operates within positions that were fixed for them. Sand versions are made to be destroyed. Several traditions build such diagrams in coloured sand over days and then sweep them away, which makes the impermanence part of the meaning, and the work exists as a process rather than as an object anybody keeps.

subject: 성곽의 곡선
title: City walls that follow the hills
content: Fortifications in several East Asian traditions run along ridgelines rather than enclosing a regular shape, so their plans are irregular curves rather than polygons. This looks unplanned and it follows a consistent logic that European bastioned fortification rejected for different reasons. Height is the resource. A wall on a ridge is harder to approach, commands the ground below, and needs to be lower to achieve the same effective height, so following the terrain saves material and gains advantage simultaneously. Builders traced the contour and let the plan take whatever shape resulted. Water and gates determine the low points. A wall must cross valleys to close the circuit, and those crossings are where streams pass and where roads enter, so the weakest points are known in advance and are given the heaviest construction. Gate structures in such walls are elaborate for exactly this reason. Curvature has a defensive value beyond the terrain. A wall that bends lets defenders on one section see and shoot along the face of another, which a straight wall prevents, so the irregularity supplies flanking fire without the projecting bastions that European engineers built for the same purpose. Construction was distributed. Sections were assigned to districts or units, each responsible for building and maintaining its portion, and inscriptions carved into the stones record who built what — which was accountability rather than decoration. Those inscriptions now let historians date sections precisely. The result reads as landscape. A wall following ridgelines is visible from far off as a line drawn along the hills, and later generations have valued that appearance, which was never among the reasons it was built that way. Walking the top is how you read them. From the wall you see the ground it was built to hold, and the reason for every bend becomes plain in a way that no map shows. Several such walls are now kept as paths for exactly that.

subject: 규방 가사의 목소리
title: Verse written in the inner rooms
content: A body of Korean verse was composed by women within households, circulated in manuscript among relatives and neighbours, and preserved outside every official channel. It survives in considerable quantity, and it records a range of experience that the formal literature of the same period omits entirely. The circumstances of composition shaped the form. Written in the vernacular script rather than in literary Chinese, in a metre that required no specialised training, and at whatever length the subject took, the form was available to anybody who could write, which is precisely why it carried voices that other forms excluded. Subjects follow a life rather than a canon. Departure from a childhood home at marriage, the labour of a household, relations with in-laws, longing for parents, illness, and instruction to daughters recur across many examples, and the frankness about hardship is considerable. Nothing in the tradition required the author to be decorous about her situation. Circulation was by copying. Works were written out by hand, given to relatives, copied again, and bound into household books, so a single composition may survive in several versions that differ in wording, and the copying itself was a social act between women in different households. Attribution is frequently lost in the chain. Collection began late and is incomplete. Because the works sat outside the literary institutions, they were not catalogued or printed, and what has been gathered came from family holdings brought forward in the twentieth century, so what survives is what particular households happened to keep. Researchers assume that a great deal more existed. Some of it is very funny. Verses about a lazy husband or a hard mother-in-law were passed round and copied out with clear relish, and the humour is one reason the books were kept at all.

subject: 발효가 만든 맛의 지역성
title: Why the same method tastes different in each place
content: Fermentation is carried out by living organisms, and which of them are present depends on where the work is done. A household using one recipe in two places gets different results, and the difference is not a mistake but the local mix of microbes doing what the recipe allows. The starting culture varies. Where a batch is begun by leaving the stuff open, whatever is in the air and on the tools takes hold, so the taste owes as much to the room as to what went in. Households that moved reported that the same preparation changed, and traditional practice held that a vessel used for years produced better results than a new one. Temperature governs which organisms dominate. A cooler place favours slower cultures that produce different compounds from those thriving in warmth, so a batch left a month in one climate is not the batch left a month in another, and traditions adjusted the timing rather than the method. Salt concentration sets the boundary. Salt suppresses most of what would spoil the food while permitting a few, so the proportion used selects which change occurs, and regional differences in saltiness match differences in what the batch becomes. Recipes specify proportion rather than taste. Vessels carry their own populations. Unglazed clay holds these living things in its pores, so a pot is passed down and prized, and scrubbing it too well was warned against. Modern practice using sterile containers and introduced cultures produces consistent results and loses exactly the variation that made regional versions distinguishable, which is a trade that producers describe openly. A batch can go wrong and often did. Households watched for signs, threw out what turned, and blamed the weather or the pot, so the craft was learned as much from failures as from any recipe.

subject: 골목의 공간 감각
title: Streets too narrow for anything but walking
content: Older settlements are threaded with lanes that no vehicle can enter, and the resulting spatial experience differs from a planned street in ways that residents describe consistently. Width, enclosure, and the absence of straight sight lines all contribute. Narrowness produces enclosure. Walls close on both sides at a distance of a few paces, so a person walking is contained rather than exposed, and the sky is a strip overhead. Residents report this as safety and visitors frequently report it as pressure, which suggests the response depends on familiarity. Bends interrupt the view. A lane that turns every twenty paces reveals itself gradually, so walking is a sequence of small discoveries rather than a traverse toward a visible destination, and the same distance feels longer than a straight equivalent. Traditions valuing this built bends deliberately in gardens. The threshold blurs. Households extend into the lane with pots, drying racks, stored goods, and seating, so the boundary between private and public is negotiated rather than drawn, and the lane functions as shared ground that everybody adjoining it maintains. This arrangement fails where residents no longer know each other. Redevelopment removes them for good reasons. Emergency vehicles cannot enter, services are hard to install, and the housing along such lanes is frequently poor, so clearance is defensible and has been carried out extensively. What is lost is documented mainly by photographers and by residents who moved, and several cities have preserved a few lanes as heritage while replacing the rest, which keeps the appearance and ends the arrangement. Cats and children use them best. A lane too narrow for a cart is wide enough for play, and the same ground serves as a route, a yard, and a meeting place through the day.

subject: 줄넘기 노래의 전승
title: Songs that pass between children and nobody else
content: Rhymes chanted while skipping rope are transmitted from child to child, without adult involvement, and they persist for remarkable periods. Collectors comparing versions across countries and decades have found the same texts with local substitutions, which makes them an unusually pure case of oral transmission. The rhythm is functional. The chant must match the rope, so the metre is fixed by the physical action rather than by any poetic convention, and rhymes that do not fit the rhythm are not used. This constraint explains why the texts across very different languages share a comparable pulse. Content is frequently nonsensical or transgressive. Rhymes name body parts, mock adults, refer to death and to courtship, and use words that children would not say in front of their parents, which is precisely the point, since the tradition belongs to a domain that adults do not supervise. Collectors have noted that children give sanitised versions when adults ask. Variation is local and rapid. Names of public figures, brands, and current events enter the rhymes within months and drop out again, so a version can be dated by its references, while the underlying structure remains stable across generations. This is the signature of a living oral tradition. Adults cannot transmit it. Attempts to teach such rhymes formally produce versions that children abandon, since what circulates is what children choose to pass on, and the selection happens entirely within a population that turns over every few years. Several documented rhymes have circulated for more than three centuries this way, without any institution preserving them. The rope sets the pace. A fast turn calls for a short line and a slow one lets a longer verse run, so the chant and the rope are chosen together and children swap both without thinking about it.

subject: 가족 초상의 배치
title: Arranging a family to be photographed
content: A family portrait places its members in a composition, and the composition makes claims about the family. Who sits and who stands, who is central, who touches whom, and who looks at the camera are all decisions, and reading them tells us how the family wished to be understood. Seating marks authority in older conventions. Elders sit while younger members stand behind, which reflects both deference and the practical fact that seated figures are lower and can be seen over, so the arrangement serves two purposes at once. Photographs from periods when this was strict show it without exception. Children are placed by size and by relationship. The youngest sit on laps or on the floor at the front, which fills the lower frame and keeps them still, and the placement of older children between adults indicates who they belong to in families that included several households. Physical contact is conventional rather than spontaneous. A hand on a shoulder appears in an enormous proportion of such photographs, and it establishes a link between two figures that the arrangement alone would not show, so photographers directed it. Its presence or absence between particular pairs has been read by historians. Absence is informative. Family portraits made after a death sometimes include a framed photograph of the missing person held by somebody, and portraits made during separations were composed to be completed later by adding a figure, which is a practice that predates photographic manipulation. Later conventions relaxed. Informal arrangements, standing groups, and candid postures replaced the tiered composition within a few decades, which records a change in how families understood their own hierarchy as much as a change in photographic fashion. Frames matter as much as the pose. A photograph hung on a wall for fifty years was seen daily by the family in it, so the choice of what to enlarge and frame was a second round of editing after the sitting.

subject: 전단의 시각 언어
title: A single sheet handed to a stranger
content: A handbill is given directly to somebody who did not ask for it, is read in seconds or discarded, and costs almost nothing to produce. These conditions have shaped the form since printing became cheap, and they produce conventions quite different from those of a poster. The message must survive a glance. A recipient decides within a moment whether to keep or drop the sheet, so the essential claim appears at the top in large type and everything else is subordinate, and sheets that bury the point are discarded unread. Distributors report this directly. Production constraints show. Printed cheaply in one or two colours on thin paper, handbills used whatever type the printer held, so the design frequently mixes several faces and sizes in a way that professional practice avoids, and that mixture became a recognisable look rather than a failure. Later designers imitated it deliberately. The medium suits urgency. Political movements, sales, performances, and warnings all use handbills because they can be produced overnight and distributed by anybody, which is why the form appears in every period of upheaval and why authorities have regulated it repeatedly. Almost none survive. Sheets are read and dropped, they were printed on paper that decays, and nobody collected them, so what remains came from people who kept examples for reasons of their own, and the surviving sample is heavily biased toward the unusual. Archives holding such material treat it as rare despite the millions printed. Its function has moved online without changing. Messages pushed to people who did not request them follow the same rules — claim first, everything else after, produced fast and discarded faster — which suggests the conventions belong to the situation rather than to the paper.

subject: 특수 효과의 역사
title: Showing what could not be filmed
content: Cinema has required images of things that do not exist since its earliest years, and the techniques developed for this form a continuous tradition from stage illusion to computation. What changed is the method rather than the problem. The first solutions were photographic tricks. Stopping the camera and altering the scene, exposing the same film twice, and running film backward all produce effects that audiences of the period found astonishing, and a magician turned filmmaker developed most of them within a decade of the medium's invention. These techniques required no equipment beyond the camera. Models and matte work carried the middle century. Miniatures photographed at a distance stand in for buildings and ships, painted glass placed before the lens supplies scenery that was never built, and areas of the frame masked during one exposure are filled during another. Each requires the camera to be locked in place, which is why films of the period cut to a static shot for such moments. Optical printing added flexibility. Rephotographing developed film permitted combinations that in-camera work could not achieve, at the cost of a generation of image quality with each pass, so effects sequences look grainier than the footage around them. Audiences learned to read that difference. Computation removed the seams and the constraints together. Elements can now be combined without generation loss and the camera can move, which eliminated the visual signature that had marked effects work for eighty years. Practitioners note that the older constraints produced restraint, since every effect was expensive and difficult, and that removing them changed what films attempt as much as how they look. The best work still hides itself. An effect that the audience notices has failed at its job, so the craft is judged by what nobody sees, which makes it hard to praise and easy to take for granted.

subject: 시장과 노점의 풍경
title: Selling from a stall that goes up each morning
content: A temporary market stall is erected, stocked, traded from, and dismantled within a day, and everything about its design follows from that cycle. What looks improvised is usually a solution refined over years by the person who sets it up. Display height is calculated. Goods sit at a level where a passer-by sees them without stooping and where the trader can reach everything from one position, so the stall is built around a standing person's arm span, and traders who set up the same arrangement daily have optimised it. Everything must pack. A stall is transported by cart, van, or on foot, so the structure folds, the goods travel in stackable containers, and the whole apparatus fits a known volume. Traders describe the packing order as fixed and the unpacking as the reverse. Cover shapes the light. An awning keeps rain off and casts a shadow that changes how goods look, which matters for food, so traders choose cloth colour deliberately and some position themselves to catch particular light. This is a judgement that permanent shops make once and market traders make daily. Position is contested and regulated. Pitches are allocated by license, seniority, or arrangement, and the difference between a good and a poor position is substantial, so disputes are common and rules about them are among the oldest in urban administration. Records of such disputes go back centuries. The form persists because it is cheap. Almost no capital is required to begin, which makes markets the entry point into trade for people with nothing, and this function has been constant across every period and place that has had them. Weather rules everything. Rain empties a market by noon, heat spoils what is not sold, and a cold day keeps buyers at home, so a trader reads the sky before deciding what to bring.

subject: 부적과 장식의 경계
title: Objects that protect and also decorate
content: Many traditional ornaments began as protective devices and continue in use after the belief has faded. Distinguishing an amulet from a decoration is frequently impossible, since the same object may be both, and the question of which it is depends on who is wearing it and when. Placement reveals intention. Protective objects are positioned where harm was thought to enter — at a threshold, over a bed, at the neck of a garment, on a child — and their location follows a logic that purely decorative placement does not, so an ornament that appears only at doorways is doing something beyond covering a surface. Materials carry the claim. Substances held to repel harm — particular metals, stones, plants, or written words — appear in such objects regardless of appearance, and an amulet may be unattractive precisely because what matters is what it is made of. Objects made from a valuable material blur the categories immediately. Text complicates the distinction further. Written charms carry words whose meaning does the work, so an object bearing them is functional to those who can read it and decorative to those who cannot, and the same object shifts category as literacy changes. Many surviving examples were made for people who could not read what they wore. Belief fades and form persists. Ornaments that everybody once understood as protective continue to be made and worn by people who could not state what they protect against, which is the ordinary trajectory, and a maker asked about the meaning may supply an explanation invented recently. Researchers treat such explanations with care. The categories were probably never clean. A person wearing something both because it is handsome and because it might help is doing what most people do, and the analytical distinction may be sharper than the practice ever was.

subject: 미술관 벽 색의 선택
title: What colour to paint the wall behind the art
content: A gallery wall is never neutral, whatever colour it is painted, since every surface reflects light onto the work and sets a comparison against which the picture is seen. Choosing that colour is a curatorial decision with consequences that visitors notice without identifying. White became standard in the twentieth century and carries its own claims. A white wall was adopted to remove distraction and to present each work as an autonomous object, which suited a period that valued exactly that, so the convention embodies an argument about what art is rather than a neutral background. Earlier galleries used dark reds and greens. Older paintings were made for coloured walls. Works painted for interiors hung with fabric or painted in deep tones were composed against those conditions, and their light passages read differently against white, so museums showing historical collections increasingly return to period colours. The change is frequently startling to regular visitors. Reflected light alters the work. A coloured wall casts a tint onto the surface of a painting, particularly at the edges and in a work with a light ground, so a red wall warms everything and a grey wall cools it. Conservators measure this and curators judge it by eye. Contrast determines how the frame reads. A dark work on a dark wall merges at the edges, which some hangs exploit to make a picture appear to float, and a light work on a light wall does the same, so the choice controls whether a viewer sees an object or a window. Practice has diverged. Contemporary galleries hold to white, historical collections have moved toward period colour, and both defend their choice on the ground that the work is being shown as it should be seen — which is the same argument reaching opposite conclusions.

subject: 소반의 지역 형태
title: A small table carried to where somebody sits
content: In traditions where meals are eaten seated on the floor, food is brought on a low individual table rather than laid on a fixed surface. The object must be light enough to carry loaded, stable on an uneven floor, and small enough to pass through a doorway held in both hands. Regional types differ in ways that specialists identify immediately. Leg form distinguishes them most clearly. Some regions made straight legs, others curved them outward in shapes named after animal limbs, and others used a solid pedestal, and the type corresponds to where the piece was made rather than to any difference in use. Collectors classify by this feature first. Wood follows the forest. Regions used what grew locally — one favouring a light softwood, another a dense hardwood, another a wood valued for its grain — so weight and colour vary regionally, and a table's material is evidence of origin independent of its shape. Proportion is fixed by the body. The top must hold a full setting within a seated person's reach, and the height must suit somebody sitting on the floor, so dimensions cluster tightly across all regional types despite the variation in everything else. The constraint is anatomical rather than cultural. Finish varied with means. Plain oiled surfaces, lacquered tops, and inlaid decoration all appear, and the same regional form exists in versions made for households of very different standing, so the type indicates place while the finish indicates wealth. Their use ended with the furniture. Households that adopted chairs and dining tables had no need for them, and the craft nearly disappeared within a generation, after which the objects were collected as folk art by people who eat at a table. They were made in pairs and sets. A household needed as many as it had members, so a run of tables from one maker shows small differences between them, and matched sets are prized for that reason.

subject: 세시 풍속의 달력
title: A year marked by what people do
content: Seasonal customs distribute observances across a year, and the pattern is not arbitrary. Occasions cluster where the agricultural and climatic year has turning points, so the calendar of customs is a record of what a farming population needed to mark, watch, or prepare for. Spring occasions concern beginnings. Rituals asking for a good year, the first ploughing, and the preparation of seed appear across many traditions at the same point, and they cluster where the work of the year actually begins rather than at any abstract new year. Communities with different climates place them differently. Summer occasions concern hazard. Observances against disease, insects, and drought fall in the months when those threats are real, and several involve washing, purification, or the display of protective objects, which corresponds to a period when illness spread and food spoiled. The timing is practical before it is symbolic. Autumn occasions concern harvest and the dead. Thanksgiving for the crop and remembrance of ancestors frequently coincide, since the harvest is when a household has something to offer, and the two functions are combined in observances across unconnected traditions. These are usually the largest occasions of the year. Winter occasions concern endurance and the turn. The longest night, the depth of cold, and the preparation for spring are marked with fire, with food stored earlier, and with gatherings, and the emphasis on light at the darkest point recurs so widely that the astronomical cause is evident. Industrial work broke the connection. Once the year's rhythm no longer followed the fields, the occasions lost their practical anchoring and survived as holidays, which is why several are now observed on fixed dates that no longer correspond to what they marked.

subject: 포스터 인쇄의 제약
title: What the printing process allowed a poster to look like
content: Poster design has always been shaped by what could be printed cheaply at large size, and the visual styles that define each period follow the technology available rather than any pure change in taste. Understanding the constraints explains the look. Stone lithography permitted large flat areas of colour. Each colour required a separate stone, drawn by hand and printed in a separate pass, so designs used few colours and bold shapes, and the registration of one pass against the next limited how fine the detail could be. The style associated with the earliest poster art follows directly from this. Colour count determined cost. Every additional colour meant another stone, another pass, and another chance of misalignment, so designers worked within three or four and used overprinting to produce further tones from those. The characteristic palettes of the period are budget decisions. Screen printing suited short runs. Ink pushed through a stencil produces dense flat colour on almost any surface, requires little equipment, and is economic for small quantities, so it became the medium of political and cultural posters produced outside commercial printing. Its look is distinct and identifiable. Photographic reproduction changed the vocabulary. Once photographs could be printed at poster scale, images replaced drawn illustration in much commercial work, and the design problem shifted from making a picture to selecting and cropping one. Designers who continued to draw did so as a choice. Digital printing removed the constraints and the discipline together. Any number of colours costs the same, runs of one are economic, and the limitations that produced the classic styles no longer exist, which is why revivals of those styles are now deliberate stylistic choices rather than the natural result of how a poster gets made. Paste and a wall did the rest. A poster was put up by hand at night, torn down by a rival, and covered by a third, so the surface of a city in any busy season was a record of that contest.

subject: 앨범과 가족의 기억
title: Deciding which photographs a family keeps
content: A family album is an edited object. Somebody chose which photographs to include, in what order, and with what captions, and the resulting book presents a version of the family rather than a record of it. Reading an album means reading those choices. Selection removes far more than it keeps. Households produced many more photographs than any album held, so the compiler discarded the unflattering, the technically poor, and frequently the people who left the family, and what remains is a curated account. Photographs excluded from albums survive in boxes when they survive at all. Sequence supplies narrative. Images are arranged chronologically in most albums, which produces a story of growth and continuity, and the events that appear — births, weddings, holidays, first days at school — are those the tradition treats as milestones. The ordinary days that made up most of a life are almost entirely absent. Captions fix meaning. A date, a place, and names written beneath a photograph determine how it is read afterwards, and an uncaptioned image becomes unidentifiable within two generations, which is why archives value annotated albums far above loose photographs. The handwriting itself becomes evidence. The compiler is usually invisible. One person in a household typically assembles the album, and that person is frequently absent from the pictures since they held the camera, so the family's record is shaped by somebody who does not appear in it. Historians studying such material now ask who did the compiling. Digital storage changed the practice fundamentally. Households now keep everything and organise nothing, so the editing that produced an album has largely stopped, and the resulting archives are larger, more complete, and considerably harder for anybody to use. Loose photographs outnumber the albums. Boxes of unsorted prints turn up in every house clearance, and archives that accept them find far more there than in the tidy books, since nobody edited them.

subject: 검무의 절제된 동작
title: A dance performed with blades
content: A Korean court dance performed with short swords combines martial gesture with strict formal restraint, and the tension between those two elements is what the form is built on. The movements suggest combat while never becoming it, and the discipline lies in that suspension. The blades are part of the instrument. Short swords with rotating handles are held so that the blade turns and catches the light with a small movement of the wrist, so the visual effect comes from the object rather than from the arm, and dancers control a flash rather than a gesture. The sound of the blades contributes as well. Restraint governs the vocabulary. Movements that would be strikes in a martial form are stopped short, redirected, or completed as circles, so the reference to combat is maintained without the aggression, and dancers describe the difficulty as holding force in reserve while appearing to release it. Formation carries the structure. Performed by several dancers in symmetrical arrangement, the piece moves through figures that mirror and oppose, so the composition rather than any individual is what the audience follows, and a court audience read the formations as they read other ceremonial arrangements. Its origins are recounted in a story about a young dancer, and historians treat that account as legend attached later to a practice that developed differently. What is documented is the court version, recorded in illustrated manuals that specify costume, weapon, and figure. Regional folk versions exist alongside the court form. They are faster, less constrained, and closer to display than to ceremony, and comparing the two shows how the same material serves entirely different occasions. Regional words went first. A term used across a whole county but absent from the book was marked as dialect within a generation, and writers who used it were read as rustic, which is how a list of words reshaped what a country could publish.

subject: 사전이 문학어에 한 일
title: What happened to a language once it was written down in one book
content: A full dictionary does more than record how words are used. It picks which uses count, fixes spellings that had wandered, and merely by existing it sets a mark against which any usage can be judged. The effects on the literature written afterwards are substantial. Spelling stabilised because a book said so. Before such books, writers spelled by ear and by habit, with wide variation inside one text, and the arrival of a list that carried weight ended that within a few lifetimes. What was chosen was frequently arbitrary, and the choices have persisted for centuries. Vocabulary was filtered. A compiler decides what goes in, and words judged coarse, local, technical, or dead were left out of most early books, so the tongue on the page was narrower than the tongue in the street, and writers who wanted standing wrote within what was listed. Regional words fell out of literary use as a direct result. Meaning acquired an official version. Where a word had been used in several ways, one entry made a single sense right, and quarrels about meaning could now be settled by looking it up rather than by arguing. Legal and technical writing depend on this. Literary consequences ran both ways. Writers gained a steady medium that readers across a wide area could share, which made a national literature possible, and they lost the freedom that variation had given, which several grumbled about at the time. Later movements deliberately reintroduced regional and spoken forms. The compilers knew what they were doing. Prefaces to early dictionaries discuss the tension between recording usage and prescribing it explicitly, and most describe themselves as recording while making choices that plainly prescribe.

subject: 자막이 화면에 하는 일
title: Reading while watching
content: Subtitles place text over a moving image, and a viewer must read and watch simultaneously. The conventions that developed for this are precise, largely invisible, and determined by how quickly people read rather than by any aesthetic preference. Reading speed sets everything. A line must remain on screen long enough to be read by a typical viewer and short enough not to persist past the moment it belongs to, which produces a maximum number of characters per second and a minimum duration per subtitle. Professional standards specify both, and violations are perceived as rushed or as lingering. Line breaks follow sense. A two line subtitle is broken where the grammar breaks, so each line is readable as a unit, and breaking mid phrase measurably slows reading. Subtitlers describe this as the most frequent error in unedited work. Condensation is unavoidable. Speech is faster than reading, so subtitles carry less than was said, and the subtitler decides what to drop — usually repetitions, hesitations, and forms of address — which means every subtitled film is also an edited one. Viewers who know both languages notice the losses. Position and contrast are functional. Text sits low so that it covers the least important part of the frame, and it is given an outline or a shadow so that it remains legible over any background, since a light subtitle over a light scene disappears entirely. Shifting a subtitle upward to avoid covering something is a deliberate choice. Same-language subtitling serves different needs. Captions for deaf viewers include speaker identification and sound description, which translation subtitles omit, so the two forms look similar and follow substantially different rules. Timing is the whole craft. A subtitle that appears a beat before the line is spoken gives away a joke, and one that lingers past a cut belongs to the wrong scene, so the work is measured in frames rather than in words.

subject: 건축 모형의 설득 기능
title: A small building made to win an argument
content: An architectural model is built before anything is constructed, and its principal function is persuasion. A client, a committee, or a public must be convinced, and the model presents a proposal in a form that drawings cannot, which is why the craft has always been closer to advocacy than to documentation. Scale determines what is shown. A model of a whole district omits detail and shows massing and relationship; one of a single building shows facade and structure; one of a room shows material and light. Choosing the scale therefore chooses the argument, since each answers a different question and leaves the others unaddressed. Material carries a claim. Models made entirely in one material — white card, pale wood, clear acrylic — present a building as pure form, which suits an argument about geometry and avoids questions about colour and texture. Models using realistic materials make a different case and invite different objections. Figures set the interpretation. Adding small human figures establishes scale and suggests use, so a plaza populated with figures appears lively while the same plaza empty appears bleak, and the choice about how many to include is a claim about what the space will become. Critics of the practice note that models are rarely as empty as the finished places. Viewpoint is controlled. A model is photographed from angles the designer selects, frequently from a height no observer will occupy, so the published images present a building as it will never be seen. Rendered images inherited this convention directly. Physical models survive as objects. Museums hold them, they are exhibited as works, and several are the only record of buildings that were never constructed, so a persuasive instrument becomes a historical document once the argument it was made for has ended.

subject: 장터의 주기
title: Markets that meet every fifth day
content: Rural markets in many regions did not open daily. They met on a cycle — every three, five, or seven days — rotating between neighbouring settlements, so a trader travelled a circuit and a household attended whichever market fell nearest. The arrangement solved a problem that a permanent market could not. Population density set the interval. A settlement large enough to support daily trade will have it; one too small must gather buyers from a wider area, and the cycle assembles enough of them in one place on one day. Regions with sparse population used longer cycles, and the interval accordingly maps onto the density. Rotation let traders work full time. A seller attending a different market each day of the cycle earns a living that no single small market could support, so the arrangement created a class of travelling traders whose routes are recorded in local histories. Their circuits linked settlements that had little other contact. The market day organised the week. Households planned purchases, sales, and journeys around it, disputes were settled there, news arrived, and arrangements were made, so the interval structured rural time more decisively than any calendar. Where markets met on the same cycle across a wide region, the whole area shared a rhythm. Location was fixed by convenience and by permission. Markets required a right granted by an authority, and disputes about who might hold one and when were common, since a market drew trade away from its neighbours. Charters recording these grants survive in quantity. Transport ended the arrangement. Once buyers could reach a permanent town market easily, the periodic ones declined, and those that survive frequently do so as occasions rather than as the principal way that a region buys and sells. The ground kept the name. Fields and squares used only on market days carry names that record the trade held there, and those names survive in places where no market has met for a century.

subject: 테두리 장식의 기능
title: The band around the edge of everything
content: Borders appear around textiles, ceramics, manuscripts, buildings, and printed pages across almost every decorative tradition, and their persistence suggests they do something structural rather than merely filling space. Several functions operate at once. A border defines the field. Marking the edge tells a viewer where the composition begins and ends, which matters most where the object continues beyond the decorated area — a woven cloth, a wall, a page — so the band converts a portion of a surface into a bounded image. Without it the design appears to have been cut off. Edges are where objects fail. Textiles fray, glazes chip, plaster cracks, and paper tears at the margins, so a border frequently coincides with reinforcement, and the decoration marks where extra material or a stronger technique was applied. The visual and the practical developed together. Repetition suits the strip. A long narrow field is naturally filled by a repeating unit, so borders across traditions use running patterns while the central field uses composed imagery, and the two therefore differ in kind rather than only in position. The border is where geometry lives. Transition is the subtler function. Between a plain ground and a busy field, or between an object and the wall it hangs on, a border mediates, and designers who remove it report that the composition sits awkwardly in its surroundings. Framing pictures performs the same job in another material. Protective meaning attaches in several traditions. A continuous band with no break was held to prevent harm from entering, which explains why certain traditions insist that a border close completely, and why a deliberate gap appears in others for the opposite reason. Weaving makes the border first. A loom builds a cloth from one end, so the band along the edge is set up before any field pattern begins, and the weaver must decide the whole design before touching the thread.

subject: 놀이와 규칙의 발명
title: Children making up the rules as they go
content: A game played by children without adult supervision is governed by rules that the players make, dispute, and revise while playing. Watching this happen shows something about how rule systems come into being that formal games conceal. Rules are stated when they are broken. Play proceeds on shared assumption until somebody does something contested, at which point a rule is articulated, argued, and settled, so the code exists mainly as a series of past decisions rather than as anything anybody wrote. Observers note that children can rarely list the rules of a game they play fluently. Fairness is negotiated continuously. Handicaps for younger or weaker players, rules about who chooses first, and permissions to retry are agreed as the situation arises, and the adjustments are frequently sophisticated, since the group's real objective is that the game continue rather than that anybody win. A game that stops being fun is renegotiated. Local variants proliferate. The same game played in two schoolyards differs in details that both groups regard as correct, and children moving between them discover this immediately, which is the same variation that folklorists document in rhymes and stories. Nothing standardises the versions. Disputes have procedures. Counting rhymes to select, forms of words that suspend play, and gestures that indicate a truce all exist to resolve conflict without an adult, and these devices are among the most widely transmitted elements of children's culture. Adults imposing rules changes the activity. Organised versions of playground games acquire fixed codes, referees, and standard equipment, and children who play both describe them as different things — which they are, since the negotiation that constituted the informal version has been removed. Adults forget how it worked. Ask anybody about a game they played daily for years and they will give you rules that their own children would dispute, since what they held was a practice rather than a code.

subject: 무대 전환의 기술
title: Changing the scene while the audience watches
content: A production that moves between locations must get from one to the next, and how it does so is a design decision with consequences for the whole evening. The options range from concealing the change entirely to making it part of the performance. Blackouts conceal and cost time. Lowering the lights hides the work and interrupts the drama, and audiences experience repeated blackouts as a stop-start rhythm, so productions using them keep them short and few. Long blackouts are among the commonest complaints in reviews of otherwise competent work. Machinery changes scenes in view. Revolving stages, tracked wagons, and flown pieces move scenery while the lights remain up, so the transition becomes something the audience watches, and directors either stage it as a moment or make it fast enough to be unremarkable. Both approaches require the machinery to be quiet. Actors performing the change is a third option. Where performers move furniture in character or in view, the transition is absorbed into the performance, which suits productions that acknowledge their own theatricality and jars in ones that do not. Companies without budget for machinery use this necessarily and frequently make a virtue of it. A single setting avoids the problem. Productions designed with one environment that serves every location shift the work from the scenery to the lighting and the text, which is how most classical drama was originally staged and how a great deal of contemporary work is staged now. Audiences accept the convention immediately. The choice signals what kind of evening it is. Elaborate transformation promises spectacle; a bare stage promises attention to the language, and a production that mismatches its transitions to its material is noticed even by audiences who could not say what was wrong.
